Lessons.Title: Add Your Way
ExplanationParagraphs: Add Your Way: use your existing knowledge of place value to add within 1,000. No single algorithm is imposed. Explain the structure of hundreds, tens and ones and choose drawings, base-ten blocks, a number line or an equation.

Warm-up — Number Talk: Hundreds, Tens, and Ones (10 minutes). Mentally compute the four source examples in order: 200+40+7=247, 50+300+2=352, 40+600+12=652, and 500+17+130=647. Display one at a time, allow silent thinking and invite multiple strategies. The extra 12 ones in the third calculation makes 40+12=52, not 42.

Activity 1 — Strategies to Add (25 minutes). Work with a partner and choose strategies for 325+102=427, 301+52=353, 276+118=394 and 298+305=603. Accessibility permits choosing three of these four; encourage the last two for comparison. Partner reasoning and diagrams are not evidenced by entering a number.

A flexible approach to 298+305 is to make a friendly number: 298+2=300, so 298+305=300+303=603. With 276+118, combine 200+100=300, 70+10=80 and 6+8=14; 300+80+14=394. Make sure that composing 14 ones is represented, not discarded.

Activity 1 synthesis: display different strategies side by side and ask which share the same underlying place-value mathematics. A base-ten diagram and expanded equations may both add like units; a number-line path and words may both add one addend to another in parts.

Activity 2 — Two Ways to Add (10 minutes). Andre and Clare both add 276+118. Andre starts with hundreds (200+100), then tens (70+10), then ones (6+8), giving 300+80+14=394. Clare adds the ones (6+8=14), tens (70+10=80), then hundreds (200+100=300), giving 14+80+300=394. Order differs but the three partial sums agree. Partners explain differences and similarities. The original lesson prepares, rather than mandates, a standard written algorithm.

Language and accessibility: MLR6 Three Reads supports comprehension of later word problems, and students can represent their reasoning by oral explanation, base-ten blocks, drawing or equations. Groups compare ways of adding; teacher reviews communication and the authenticity of each explanation.

Synthesis: reflect on your preferred representation for adding and when you would change your method for different numbers. Base-ten blocks are required materials. Optional centers are Target Numbers stage 6, Five in a Row stage 8 and Rectangle Rumble stage 2 with teacher-authorized original materials, not copied here.

Independent Edulytics practice and Cool-down are original checks of adding within 1,000; they are not the publisher-gated Add It Up task. The original PDF and source photograph have not been independently rendered, so full source-material parity is explicitly unclaimed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Place-value partition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A three-digit number can be expressed as hundreds, tens and ones.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add quantities by like units, then combine partial sums.

KeyConcepts.Title: Flexible compatible numbers
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding near-round numbers can simplify a calculation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compensate precisely for any change to an addend.

KeyConcepts.Title: Commutativity and associativity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Reordering or regrouping the same addends leaves a sum unchanged.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep the exact original parts when switching order.

WorkedExamples.Title: Value of a nonstandard expanded sum
WorkedExamples.Question: Mentally calculate 40+600+12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Combine tens and ones after identifying the hundreds.

WorkedExamples.Title: Add by like place-value units
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate 276+118 using any place-value strategy.
WorkedExamples.Method: Separate the hundreds, tens and ones.
Steps: Explain how 14 ones is equivalent to one ten and four ones.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The 12 ones were treated as only two ones.
Discarding 10 loses a ten from the total.
Increasing one addend alone changes the sum.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming Andre and Clare must use the same order.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Their partial sums are identical even though the sequence differs.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare the parts, not the order of recording.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling an automatically checked sum proof of discussion participation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source asks for multiple methods, choice of tasks and partner explanations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher rubric for drawings, strategies and conversations.

SummaryPoints: For 276+118, Andre and Clare obtain the same three partial sums in different orders.
The original task explicitly permits selecting three of four sums for accessibility.
Explain strategies and compare representations; a scalar answer alone is insufficient.
No source PDF, original photo, gated publisher Cool-down or gameboard parity has been claimed.
